title: Extensive Reading — A Full Programme

pts: Extensive reading's benefits — vocabulary growth, reading speed, general proficiency — depend substantially on sustained volume, not occasional exposure.
A programme of regular, graded reading consistently outperforms sporadic, unstructured reading in research findings.
This is the practical argument for scheduling reading time, not just assigning it as homework.

pts: Easy, self-selected material read at a comfortable pace with no follow-up test defines a genuine extensive reading programme.
Reading should be for pleasure and general understanding, not for detailed comprehension-check purposes.
Deviating too far from these principles — adding quizzes, forcing unwanted titles — tends to undermine the programme's core benefits.
points.who: Day & Bamford's ten principles for extensive reading

v: A paraphrased list of the ten principles

items: In pairs, describe how reading is currently used in your school: what is read, when, how it is checked.
Read a summary of Day and Bamford’s (2002) principles.

blocks.x: Core principles, paraphrased: the material is easy and varied; learners choose; they read as much as possible, for pleasure and general understanding; reading is its own reward, usually fast, individual and silent; the teacher guides and is a role model of a reader. A typical conflict: Every learner reads the same prescribed supplementary reader and answers ten questions per chapter. This contradicts choice, ease and ‘reading is its own reward’. It is intensive reading under another name.

body: Purpose: to present the principles as a path. Content: ten stepping stones across a stream, each with a short label, leading from a learner holding a book to a far bank marked ‘reading habit’. Style: gentle, illustrated. Board version: ten numbered circles in a line.

points.sub: Right below, not at, current level
pts: Material at roughly one level below a learner's current proficiency (the 'i-1' level) supports the fluent, enjoyable reading extensive reading requires.
Too-difficult material collapses into intensive reading by necessity, losing extensive reading's distinct benefits.
Graded reader series calibrated to CEFR levels make this selection process practical to manage at scale.

v: Graded readers or short books at different levels

items: Learners open a book at any page and read it.
They fold down one finger for each unknown word.
None or one finger: probably right for extensive reading.
Two or three: better for study with support.
More: put it back and try an easier book, without shame.
Colour-coded dots on spines help younger learners choose quickly.
Support: the teacher pre-selects three suitable books.
Challenge: learners explain in English why a book is or is not right for them.

blocks.x: The test is a rule of thumb. Research suggests that comfortable reading needs around 98 per cent of running words known (Hu and Nation 2000), roughly one unknown word in fifty.

lines: T: Good that you noticed. Try one from the green box. Extensive reading should feel easy.

blocks.x: Day and Bamford (1998) call this reading at ‘i minus 1’: just below the learner’s level, so attention goes to meaning and enjoyment. Too-hard books force slow, word-by-word decoding, and the extensive benefit is lost.

body: Purpose: to teach self-selection. Content: an open book beside three hands: no fingers folded (‘Easy reading’), two folded (‘Study book’), five folded (‘Not yet’). Style: clear, child-friendly. Board version: three drawn hands.

pts: Dedicate regular, protected class time to reading, not only homework time competing with other priorities.

pts: Extensive reading is one of the most effective vehicles for the incidental vocabulary learning described in Unit 5.
Repeated exposure to words in varied, natural contexts builds the depth of knowledge single-exposure teaching cannot.
This makes extensive reading a direct, low-effort complement to explicit vocabulary teaching, not a competitor to it.

In review, learners compare how each word was used and which words appeared with it.
Each learner shares one ‘word I met three times’ a week.
Support: look for one word only.
Challenge: note collocations (heavy rain, make a decision) for a class list.

dek: Unit 31 of 100: moving extensive reading from an occasional homework suggestion (Tier I) into a scheduled, structured, and genuinely effective programme.

aims.x: This unit turns extensive reading from an occasional suggestion into a planned programme. Unit 5 introduced graded readers as a source of incidental vocabulary, and Unit 19 treated reading as part of self-study. Here the question is organizational: how does a teacher build a programme that runs all year, with protected time, a real library and light accountability?
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain why the benefits of extensive reading depend on volume;
apply Day and Bamford’s principles when designing a programme;
match learners to books slightly below their current level;
schedule and protect regular reading time;
track reading without testing comprehension;
plan a low-cost class library, print or digital;
respond clearly to common objections.

why: Why this matters. Extensive reading's benefits are well-evidenced, but only when run as a structured programme — an occasional reader assigned once a term rarely delivers them.

background.x: Most teachers agree that reading is good for language learners. Far fewer run a reading programme. The difference matters, because the research describes the effects of sustained reading: many books, read over months, at an easy level. An early, influential study is Elley and Mangubhai’s (1983) ‘book flood’ in Fijian primary schools, where classes given high-interest storybooks and time to read them made clear gains compared with classes following the usual programme. A later meta-analysis supports a positive effect of extensive reading on reading proficiency, while noting that studies vary widely in design (Jeon and Day 2016).

Richard Day and Julian Bamford (1998) gave the field its practical shape. They defined extensive reading as reading large quantities of easy, self-selected material for pleasure and general understanding, and later set out ten principles for teaching it (Day and Bamford 2002). Nation and Waring (2020) explain how graded readers work and how to organize a programme. Reading builds fluency and vocabulary only when learners understand almost everything on the page. Christine Nuttall (2005) described the ‘vicious circle’ of the weak reader, who reads slowly, does not enjoy it, reads little and so stays slow, and the ‘virtuous circle’ in which enjoyment leads to more reading and more reading to greater ease.

In India, this connects directly to policy. The NEP 2020 calls for a culture of reading, well-stocked libraries and enjoyable books in all languages (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020), and the NCF 2023 treats reading for pleasure as central to literacy (NCERT 2023). A programme can be multilingual: learners who read widely in Kannada, Tamil or Urdu bring habits and background knowledge that transfer to English. Many schools face small book budgets, locked cupboards, classes of fifty and a strong exam culture. This unit works within those constraints.

items: Reading volume. Pages or books per term from logs, as evidence of habit, not a mark.
Reading rate. A timed, easy passage once a term to see whether speed is rising (Nation and Waring 2020).
Book talk observation. A checklist: can the learner summarize and recommend a book?
Attitude survey. An anonymous question on reading enjoyment at the start and end of the year.
How much do your learners actually read in English in a typical week?
Which of Day and Bamford’s principles does your practice contradict?
What happens in your school to books that are ‘too good to lend’?
How could you protect reading time when the portion is behind?
How do you show learners that you are a reader?
Which home-language books could sit beside English books in your library?

terms.def: A programme that supplies classrooms with many high-interest books and time to read them; in Fiji, it produced clear gains in reading (Elley and Mangubhai 1983).
A short, enthusiastic presentation about a book by a teacher or learner, intended to interest others in reading it; regular book talks help build a reading culture in class.

Reading large quantities of easy, self-selected material for pleasure and general understanding, such as graded readers or StoryWeaver books (Day and Bamford 1998). It builds fluency, vocabulary and reading habits.
A book written or adapted for language learners within a controlled range of vocabulary and grammar, used for extensive reading at the right level.
Reading material just below the learner’s current level, so that attention can go to meaning and enjoyment. It is the recommended level for extensive reading (Day and Bamford 1998).
Close, detailed reading of a short text, often with attention to vocabulary, grammar and meaning, as distinct from extensive reading for pleasure.

A simple record in which learners note what they have read, for how long and a brief response. It supports extensive reading and self-study, and helps the teacher monitor quantity and enjoyment without formal testing.

A regular period in which everyone, including the teacher, reads self-chosen material silently without tasks or tests. It builds reading habits and fluency, and is often used within an extensive reading programme.
The positive cycle in which enjoyment of reading leads to more reading, which leads to greater ease and further enjoyment (Nuttall 2005). It contrasts with the vicious circle of the weak reader.
The proportion of words in a text that a reader knows, used to judge whether a text suits a learner’s level. Extensive reading generally needs very high coverage, around 98 per cent (Nation 2006).
